title: Docker Complete Handbook
summary: A start-to-finish Docker series: architecture, images and containers, Dockerfile and build optimization, storage, networking, Compose, registries, security, debugging, production orchestration, best practices and interview prep.

chapters.title: Docker Complete Handbook
points: What Docker is: a platform that packages an app and its dependencies into portable containers
Containers vs virtual machines in one line: shared host kernel vs a full guest OS
The problem it solves: 'works on my machine' becomes the same image everywhere
Roadmap of the series: architecture, images, Dockerfile, storage, networking, Compose, registries, security, debugging, production, interview prep

chapters.title: Docker Architecture and Engine Internals
points: Client-server model: the docker CLI talks to the dockerd daemon over a REST API
Default socket is /var/run/docker.sock; DOCKER_HOST or a context points the CLI at a remote daemon
dockerd delegates to containerd, which manages the container lifecycle and images
containerd starts containers through runc, the OCI runtime that calls the kernel
containerd-shim keeps a container alive and its stdio open even if dockerd restarts
Namespaces isolate what a process sees: pid, net, mnt, uts, ipc, user
cgroups limit what a process uses: CPU, memory, block I/O, pids
Union filesystem (overlay2) stacks read-only layers under one writable layer
Comparison: container shares the host kernel and starts in milliseconds; a VM boots its own kernel and takes seconds to minutes
Example: docker run -d nginx triggers CLI, dockerd, containerd, shim, runc, and the nginx process
Mistake: mounting docker.sock into a container hands that container root-equivalent control of the host
Interview Point: Walk through what happens on docker run. How do namespaces differ from cgroups? Why does Docker use containerd and runc? Is a container a lightweight VM?

chapters.title: Images and Layers
points: An image is an immutable, layered filesystem plus metadata (config, entrypoint, env)
Each Dockerfile filesystem instruction (RUN, COPY, ADD) creates a layer; layers are content-addressed by SHA256 digest
Layers are shared across images and cached, saving disk and pull time
An image manifest lists the config blob and layer digests; a manifest list (index) handles multi-architecture images
Tags are mutable pointers; a digest (image@sha256:...) is immutable and exact
docker image ls, docker history and docker image inspect show size, layers and config
Comparison: image (read-only template) vs container (running instance with a writable layer)
Comparison: base images, alpine is small but uses musl libc, debian-slim is a compat middle ground, distroless has no shell or package manager, scratch is empty
Example: docker pull node:22-alpine, then docker history node:22-alpine to see each layer's size
Mistake: relying on the latest tag, which breaks reproducibility and moves without warning
Mistake: deleting a file in a later layer does not shrink the image, the earlier layer still holds it
Interview Point: What is a layer and how is it cached? Tag vs digest, which is safer to deploy? How does a multi-arch image work? How do you shrink an image?

chapters.title: Containers and the Lifecycle
points: A container is a running (or stopped) instance of an image: an isolated process with its own filesystem, network and process tree
Lifecycle states: created, running, paused, exited, removed
docker run = create + start; docker stop sends SIGTERM, waits 10s, then SIGKILL
docker kill sends SIGKILL immediately; docker rm deletes a stopped container; --rm auto-removes on exit
Key run flags: -d, -it, -p, -v, -e, --name, --restart, --memory, --cpus
Restart policies: no, on-failure[:max], always, unless-stopped
Resource limits use cgroups: --memory=512m, --cpus=1.5; exceeding memory gets the process OOM-killed (exit code 137)
The container's main process is PID 1; the container exits when PID 1 exits
Comparison: docker exec runs a new process in a running container, docker attach connects to PID 1's stdio
Comparison: ENTRYPOINT is the fixed executable, CMD supplies default arguments that docker run can override
Example: docker run -d --name web --restart unless-stopped -p 8080:80 --memory 256m nginx
Mistake: a shell-form CMD makes sh PID 1, so SIGTERM never reaches your app; use exec form or --init
Interview Point: What happens on docker stop? Why does the container exit immediately? ENTRYPOINT vs CMD? What does exit code 137 mean?

chapters.title: Dockerfile Essentials
points: A Dockerfile is a text recipe of ordered instructions that docker build turns into an image
FROM picks the base image; WORKDIR sets the working directory and creates it
COPY copies files from the build context into the image; ADD also extracts local tars and fetches URLs
RUN executes at build time and creates a layer; CMD and ENTRYPOINT define runtime behavior
ENV persists in the image and the container; ARG exists only at build time
EXPOSE documents a port but does not publish it; -p does the publishing
USER switches to a non-root user; HEALTHCHECK defines a liveness probe command
LABEL attaches metadata, VOLUME declares a mount point, STOPSIGNAL sets the stop signal
Comparison: COPY vs ADD, prefer COPY unless you need tar extraction
Comparison: exec form ['node','app.js'] vs shell form node app.js, exec form gets signals directly
Example: FROM node:22-alpine / WORKDIR /app / COPY package*.json ./ / RUN npm ci / COPY . . / USER node / CMD ['node','server.js']
Mistake: putting secrets in ENV or ARG, they stay readable in docker history and image inspect
Interview Point: ARG vs ENV? COPY vs ADD? What does EXPOSE actually do? CMD vs ENTRYPOINT in a Dockerfile?

chapters.title: Build Cache and Multi-Stage Builds
points: The build cache reuses a layer when the instruction and its inputs are unchanged
Cache invalidation cascades: once one layer changes, every layer after it rebuilds
Order instructions from least to most frequently changing: dependencies first, source code last
Copy only the manifest (package.json, go.mod, requirements.txt) before installing dependencies to keep that layer cached
The .dockerignore file shrinks the build context and stops node_modules, .git and .env entering the image
Multi-stage builds use several FROM lines and COPY --from=builder to ship only the final artifact
Build stages hold compilers and dev tools; the runtime stage holds only the binary and runtime
BuildKit adds parallel stages, skipping unused stages and cache mounts (RUN --mount=type=cache)
BuildKit secret mounts (RUN --mount=type=secret) use credentials at build time without leaving them in a layer
Comparison: single-stage Go image of about 800 MB vs multi-stage with scratch or distroless at 10-20 MB
Example: FROM golang:1.23 AS build / RUN go build -o app / FROM gcr.io/distroless/static / COPY --from=build /src/app /app
Mistake: COPY . . before installing dependencies busts the cache on every code change
Mistake: chaining RUN apt-get update and apt-get install in separate layers leaves a stale cache; combine them and clean /var/lib/apt/lists
Interview Point: Why does instruction order matter? How do multi-stage builds cut image size? What is BuildKit? How do you pass secrets safely at build time?

chapters.title: Volumes and Storage
points: The container's writable layer is deleted with the container, so data there is ephemeral
Volumes are Docker-managed storage under /var/lib/docker/volumes, independent of the container lifecycle
Bind mounts map a host path into the container, tying it to the host's directory layout
tmpfs mounts live in host memory only, useful for sensitive or scratch data
Comparison: named volume (portable, managed, best for databases) vs bind mount (dev code reload) vs tmpfs (in-memory, never on disk)
Prefer --mount (explicit, errors on a missing path) over -v (silently creates a missing host directory)
Mount flags: ro for read-only, volume drivers (local, NFS, cloud plugins) for remote storage
A new empty named volume is populated from the image's existing content at that path; a bind mount hides it
Volume commands: docker volume create, ls, inspect, rm, prune
Backup pattern: run a throwaway container that mounts the volume and tars it to a bind mount
Example: docker run -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:16 keeps the database across container deletion
Mistake: docker volume prune or docker system prune --volumes silently deletes unused data volumes
Mistake: a bind mount over the app directory hides the files built into the image
Interview Point: Volume vs bind mount, when would you use each? How do you persist database data? Where is data written in a container by default? How do you back up a volume?

chapters.title: Docker Networking
points: Each container gets its own network namespace, a virtual interface and an IP address
Bridge is the default driver: containers on one host talk through a virtual switch (docker0)
Host driver shares the host network stack: no isolation, no port mapping needed
None driver gives only loopback: full network isolation
Overlay connects containers across multiple hosts (Swarm), using VXLAN
Macvlan gives a container its own MAC and an address on the physical LAN
User-defined bridge networks provide automatic DNS resolution by container name; the default bridge does not
Publishing a port: -p 8080:80 maps host port 8080 to container port 80 via iptables NAT rules
Port binding to a specific interface: -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80 keeps the service off the public interface
Containers on different user-defined networks cannot reach each other; attach to both to bridge
Example: docker network create app; docker run -d --network app --name db postgres; app connects to host db:5432
Mistake: -p 5432:5432 on a database exposes it to the whole network, and Docker's iptables rules bypass many host firewalls (ufw)
Mistake: connecting to localhost inside a container reaches the container itself, not the host or another service
Interview Point: Bridge vs host vs overlay? How do containers find each other by name? How does port publishing work? Why can't a container reach the default bridge's containers by name?

chapters.title: Docker Compose
points: Compose defines a multi-container application in one compose.yaml and runs it with docker compose up
Top-level keys: services, networks, volumes, configs, secrets
Each service sets image or build, ports, environment, volumes, depends_on, restart and healthcheck
Compose creates a default network per project, and services reach each other by service name
depends_on with condition: service_healthy waits for a healthcheck; plain depends_on only orders startup
Environment: environment, env_file and ${VAR} interpolation from a .env file
Profiles (profiles: [debug]) enable optional services only when requested
Override files: compose.override.yaml is merged automatically; use -f to layer compose.prod.yaml
Core commands: up -d, down (-v also removes volumes), ps, logs -f, exec, build, config
docker compose watch syncs or rebuilds on file changes for a fast dev loop
Comparison: Compose (single host, dev and small deployments) vs Swarm or Kubernetes (multi-host orchestration)
Example: services web (build: ., ports 8000:8000, depends_on db healthy) and db (postgres:16, volume pgdata, healthcheck pg_isready)
Mistake: docker compose down -v deletes named volumes and the data in them
Interview Point: What does depends_on guarantee? How do services discover each other? How do you manage dev vs prod config? Is Compose production-ready?

chapters.title: Registries and Image Distribution
points: A registry stores and serves images; a repository holds the versions (tags) of one image
Image name anatomy: registry/namespace/repository:tag, Docker Hub is the default registry
Docker Hub, GitHub Container Registry, Amazon ECR, Google Artifact Registry, Azure ACR and self-hosted Harbor are common choices
docker login stores credentials in ~/.docker/config.json; use a credential helper instead of plain text
Push flow: docker build -t, docker tag, docker push; pull flow: docker pull, then layers download in parallel
Only missing layers are transferred, so pushes and pulls reuse shared layers
Tagging strategy: immutable version tags (1.4.2), git SHA tags for traceability, avoid deploying a mutable latest
Docker Hub applies pull-rate limits to anonymous and free users; use authenticated pulls or a mirror
A pull-through cache (registry mirror) speeds up CI and reduces rate-limit pressure
Private registries: run registry:2 or Harbor for scanning, RBAC and replication
Example: docker tag app:1.0 ghcr.io/acme/app:1.0 && docker push ghcr.io/acme/app:1.0
Mistake: pushing an image with baked-in secrets to a public repository
Interview Point: How do tag and digest differ in deployment? How do you speed up CI pulls? How do you set up a private registry? What gets uploaded on a push?

chapters.title: Container Security
points: Containers share the host kernel, so isolation is weaker than a VM: a kernel exploit can escape
Run as a non-root user (USER in the Dockerfile, --user at runtime); root in a container is root on bind-mounted files
User namespace remapping and rootless Docker map container root to an unprivileged host user
Drop capabilities: --cap-drop ALL then --cap-add only what is needed; NET_BIND_SERVICE, for example
Never use --privileged: it grants all capabilities and device access
Read-only root filesystem: --read-only with tmpfs for writable paths
Seccomp and AppArmor or SELinux profiles restrict system calls and file access; Docker ships a default seccomp profile
--security-opt no-new-privileges blocks privilege escalation through setuid binaries
Scan images for CVEs (Docker Scout, Trivy, Grype) in CI and fail builds on critical findings
Pin base images by digest, use minimal distroless images, and generate an SBOM; sign images with cosign or Docker Content Trust
Handle secrets with BuildKit secret mounts, Swarm or Compose secrets, or an external vault, not ENV
Comparison: root container (full host impact on escape) vs rootless + dropped caps + read-only fs (small blast radius)
Mistake: mounting /var/run/docker.sock into a container grants host control
Interview Point: How do you harden a container? Why is --privileged dangerous? How are secrets handled in builds and runtime? What does rootless mode change?

chapters.title: Debugging and Troubleshooting
points: Start with docker ps -a and docker logs --tail 100 -f to see state and output
docker inspect returns the full JSON: state, exit code, mounts, networks, env and health
Exit codes: 0 clean, 1 app error, 125 daemon error, 126 not executable, 127 command not found, 137 SIGKILL or OOM, 143 SIGTERM
docker exec -it <c> sh opens a shell; if the image has none, use docker debug or attach a sidecar with --pid and --network
docker stats and docker top show live CPU, memory and processes
docker events streams daemon activity such as die, oom and health_status
docker inspect --format '{{.State.OOMKilled}}' confirms an out-of-memory kill
Networking checks: docker network inspect, exec ping or curl to the service name, verify port mapping with docker port
Build failures: docker build --progress=plain --no-cache shows full output and rules out stale cache
Crash loop: override the entrypoint (--entrypoint sh) to inspect the image without running the app
docker system df shows disk use; docker system prune frees dangling images, stopped containers and build cache
Comparison: docker logs (stdout/stderr only) vs files written inside the container, so log to stdout
Mistake: assuming 'Exited (0)' is a failure when PID 1 simply finished its work
Interview Point: A container exits immediately, how do you debug it? How do you find an OOM kill? How do you debug a distroless image with no shell? What fills up /var/lib/docker?

chapters.title: Production and Orchestration
points: Production needs scheduling, scaling, self-healing, rolling updates, service discovery and secret management beyond a single host
Docker Swarm is built in: docker swarm init, services, replicas and an overlay network
Swarm commands: docker service create --replicas 3, docker service scale, docker service update for rolling updates
Kubernetes is the industry standard: pods, deployments, services, ingress, and a large ecosystem
Comparison: Compose (one host) vs Swarm (simple clustering) vs Kubernetes (feature-rich, steeper learning curve)
Always set resource limits and memory reservations so one container cannot starve the host
Healthchecks drive restarts and traffic routing; readiness vs liveness matters on Kubernetes
Logging: send stdout/stderr to a driver (json-file with max-size and max-file, or fluentd, loki, awslogs) so logs do not fill the disk
Make containers stateless: externalize state to volumes, databases or object storage
Deploy by immutable image tag or digest, with rolling or blue-green updates and a rollback path
Graceful shutdown: handle SIGTERM and set a stop_grace_period long enough to drain connections
Example: docker service create --name web --replicas 3 --update-parallelism 1 -p 80:80 myapp:1.4.2
Mistake: no log rotation on json-file fills the disk and takes the host down
Interview Point: When do you move from Compose to Kubernetes? How do rolling updates and rollbacks work? How do you handle persistent state? How do you ship container logs?

chapters.title: Best Practices and Common Mistakes
points: One process per container, composed into services, for clean scaling and logs
Use small, trusted, version-pinned base images and rebuild regularly for security patches
Use multi-stage builds, .dockerignore and ordered layers for small, fast builds
Run as non-root, drop capabilities and keep the root filesystem read-only where possible
Keep containers stateless and ephemeral; persist data in volumes
Configure through environment variables or secret mounts, never hard-code credentials
Add a HEALTHCHECK and handle SIGTERM for graceful shutdown
Log to stdout and rotate logs
Comparison: good Dockerfile (pinned tag, cached deps, non-root, slim) vs bad Dockerfile (latest, COPY . . first, root, build tools shipped)
Example: replace RUN apt-get install -y curl git vim with only the packages needed plus --no-install-recommends and cache cleanup
Mistake: treating a container like a VM: SSH inside, manual edits and long-lived patched state
Mistake: building the image on the production server instead of pulling a CI-built, scanned image
Interview Point: What are your top Dockerfile best practices? Why one process per container? Why not SSH into containers? How do you keep images reproducible?

chapters.title: Docker Interview Questions
points: Q: Container vs VM? A: shared kernel and process isolation via namespaces and cgroups, versus full guest OS on a hypervisor
Q: Image vs container? A: an immutable layered template versus a running instance with a writable layer
Q: ENTRYPOINT vs CMD? A: ENTRYPOINT fixes the executable; CMD gives default arguments that run-time args replace
Q: COPY vs ADD? A: COPY is plain copy; ADD also extracts local tars and fetches URLs, so prefer COPY
Q: How do you reduce image size? A: slim or distroless base, multi-stage builds, combined RUN steps, .dockerignore
Q: Volume vs bind mount? A: managed and portable versus a host-path mapping for development
Q: How do containers communicate? A: user-defined bridge network with DNS by name; overlay across hosts
Q: How does layer caching work? A: unchanged instruction and inputs reuse the layer, and a change invalidates everything after it
Q: How do you debug a crashing container? A: logs, inspect, exit code, events, override the entrypoint to get a shell
Q: How do you secure containers? A: non-root, dropped capabilities, read-only fs, scanned and signed images, no docker.sock mount
Q: Compose vs Kubernetes? A: single-host definition versus a multi-host orchestrator with self-healing and scaling
Interview Point: Be ready to explain the docker run flow, a Dockerfile review, a debugging scenario and a production rollout end to end

chapters.title: Docker Cheatsheet
points: Images: docker build -t name:tag . | pull | push | tag | rmi | image prune | history | inspect
Containers: docker run -d --name n -p h:c -v v:/path -e K=V --restart unless-stopped img
Manage: ps -a | stop | start | restart | rm -f | logs -f --tail 100 | exec -it c sh | cp | stats | top
Volumes: docker volume create | ls | inspect | rm | prune; --mount type=volume,src=v,dst=/d
Networks: docker network create | ls | inspect | connect | disconnect; -p host:container
Compose: docker compose up -d | down | ps | logs -f | exec | build | config | watch
Dockerfile order: FROM, WORKDIR, COPY manifest, RUN install, COPY source, USER, EXPOSE, HEALTHCHECK, CMD
Exit codes: 0 ok, 1 app error, 126/127 command problems, 137 SIGKILL/OOM, 143 SIGTERM
Security: --user, --cap-drop ALL, --read-only, no-new-privileges, scan with Trivy or Scout
Cleanup: docker system df | system prune | builder prune; add --volumes with caution
Debug: logs, inspect, events, exec, --progress=plain --no-cache, --entrypoint sh
